entries.title: Bengali at a glance
body: Bengali (Bangla) is an Indo-Aryan language with around 270 million speakers, the national language of Bangladesh and the language of West Bengal, Tripura and parts of Assam in India. It has a long literary tradition; Rabindranath Tagore wrote in Bengali, including the national anthems of both Bangladesh and India.
The verb comes last, there is no grammatical gender, and verbs change for person and for three levels of politeness. Postpositions and case endings follow the noun.

entries.title: How the script works
body: Bengali is written in the Bengali–Assamese script, an abugida like Devanagari: each consonant carries a built-in short vowel, said o (ক = ko), and other vowels are marks around the consonant. A full vowel letter is used at the start of a word.
Most letters hang from a line along the top. The hasanta ্ removes the built-in vowel, and consonant clusters are often written as joined letters (যুক্তাক্ষর).

entries.title: Sounds to watch
entries.body: The built-in vowel অ is said like the o in “hot”, not like Hindi's a. Long and short vowels are written differently but usually sound the same. Bengali has breathy consonants (kh, gh, ch, jh, th, dh, ph, bh) and retroflex ones made with the tongue curled back (ট, ড). শ, ষ and স are usually all said sh.

entries.title: Pronouns and politeness
entries.body: “You” and “he / she” come in levels of respect, and the verb ending follows the level. There is no he / she difference.

entries.title: The simple present
entries.body: Verbs are listed by their verbal noun (করা, to do). Take off -া and add the ending. The verb does not change for plural subjects.

entries.title: Noun endings
entries.body: Endings attach directly to the noun. -টা / -টি make it definite, and the case endings follow.

entries.title: Numbers and Bengali digits
entries.body: Bengali has its own digits, used on signs, prices and dates alongside 0–9. Numbers up to a hundred each have their own word and are best learned one by one.

entries.title: Language Movement Day
entries.body: On 21 February 1952 students in Dhaka were killed while demonstrating for Bengali to be an official language of Pakistan. The day, Ekushey February, is remembered in Bangladesh at the Shaheed Minar, and UNESCO made 21 February International Mother Language Day.
